title: Minimum Jumps to Target With Forbidden
description:
# Minimum Jumps to Target With Forbidden

You start at position `0` on a number line. In one move, you may jump forward by exactly `a` or backward by exactly `b`.

Some positions are forbidden and may never be visited. You also may not make two backward jumps in a row. Return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach position `x`, or `-1` if reaching `x` is impossible.

## Example 1:

**Input:** forbidden = [14,4,18,1,15], a = 3, b = 15, x = 9
**Output:** 3

One shortest path is `0 -> 3 -> 6 -> 9`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** forbidden = [8,3,16,6,12,20], a = 15, b = 13, x = 11
**Output:** -1

## Important Details

Positions below `0` are forbidden. You may jump beyond the target and come back, but never land on a forbidden position or make two backward jumps consecutively.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= forbidden.length <= 1000`
* `1 <= a, b, x <= 2000`
* `0 <= forbidden[i] <= 2000`
* All forbidden positions are distinct.
* `forbidden[i] != 0`.

solutions.name: BFS With Direction State
solutions.description:
## Approach

Run BFS over states `(position, previousMoveWasBackward)`. From each state, the forward jump always goes to `(position + a, false)`. The backward jump is allowed only when the previous move was not backward, and it goes to `(position - b, true)`. Track forbidden positions and a finite upper bound so the queue cannot grow forever.

## Key Insight

The same position is not enough to describe the future. If you reached position `p` by a forward jump, a backward jump may be legal next; if you reached `p` by a backward jump, another backward jump is illegal. Therefore the visited set must distinguish those two states.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(U)
- Space Complexity: O(U)

Here `U` is the chosen finite search bound.

solutions.name: Level-Order BFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Process the BFS queue one level at a time. Each outer-loop iteration represents one more jump. Store states as encoded integers so the visited set is compact, and stop immediately when the current level reaches `x`.

## Key Insight

BFS levels correspond exactly to jump counts in an unweighted graph. The first time a target state is removed from the queue, the current level is the minimum number of jumps.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(U)
- Space Complexity: O(U)

solutions.name: Reverse State BFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Search the directed state graph backward. Start from both possible target states `(x, false)` and `(x, true)`. A reverse step into a state whose previous move was forward can come from either previous direction at `position - a`; a reverse step into a state whose previous move was backward must come from `(position + b, false)`. Stop when the original start state `(0, false)` is reached.

## Key Insight

The graph is directed because backward jumps cannot repeat. Reversing the edges is still valid if the direction flag is interpreted as part of the state, and it provides an independent way to reason about the same shortest-path structure.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(U)
- Space Complexity: O(U)

solutions.name: Bidirectional State BFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Run BFS from the start state and from the two target states at the same time. The start side expands normal outgoing moves, while the target side expands reversed incoming moves. Always expand the smaller frontier and stop when the two visited regions meet.

## Key Insight

For directed graphs, bidirectional BFS must use outgoing edges on the start side and incoming edges on the target side. Keeping the direction flag inside the encoded state makes those two edge generators precise and prevents illegal repeated-backward paths from leaking into the search.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(U)
- Space Complexity: O(U)
